summary:
Thomas Cresap (c.1694–c.1790) was an English-born Maryland settler and trader who took part in colonial boundary disputes and westward expansion. He emigrated at 15 and became an agent for Lord Baltimore, asserting Maryland’s claims in the Susquehanna Valley against Pennsylvania settlers. Cresap and his men used force in the conflict known as Cresap’s War. Pennsylvania’s sheriff arrested him in 1736; he was released around 1738, and King George II later ordered the boundary dispute settled.

Cresap moved west, establishing trading posts along Antietam Creek and near present-day Cumberland. In 1748–1750, he and Delaware chief Nemacolin widened a Native American trail from Cumberland to Redstone into a wagon road. Cresap and his sons later raised troops during the French and Indian War.

His son Michael continued the family’s Indian trade. In 1774, Michael was mistakenly accused of leading killings of Native Americans that helped provoke frontier retaliation and Lord Dunmore’s War. Cresap died in Allegany County, Maryland, aged about 88.
